title: Why a Weaker Russia Keeps Fighting
gist: A paywalled teaser: the accessible portion reports Putin's end-of-June 2026 interview claiming Russia is winning along a roughly 800-mile front while dismissing Ukrainian deep-strike drone attacks on Russian oil refineries as having no effect. The Carnegie authors' framing is that Putin sees little need to negotiate; the analytical argument for why a materially weaker Russia still fights is cut off by the paywall.

insights.claim: In an interview at the end of June 2026, Vladimir Putin declared that Russia would win its war against Ukraine, claiming the Russian army was advancing along the roughly 800-mile frontline and occupying more Ukrainian land every day while Kyiv was flailing.
insights.speaker: Alexander Gabuev
insights.so_what: Public confidence from the Kremlin at this stage argues against near-term ceasefire pricing in European risk assets, Ukrainian debt, or grain and energy corridors.
insights.locator: At the end of June, Russian President Vladimir Putin

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone strikes have been torching Russian oil refineries and other critical infrastructure deep behind the frontlines, a campaign Putin conceded is creating problems even while publicly dismissing it.
insights.speaker: Alexander Gabuev
insights.so_what: Sustained refinery strikes constrain Russian product exports and domestic fuel supply — the most direct channel through which the war still moves crack spreads and diesel markets.
insights.locator: He acknowledged that the Ukrainian drone strikes

insights.claim: Putin publicly framed Ukraine's deep-strike campaign as irrelevant, saying the attacks have no impact whatsoever on the situation and that Russians would adapt and persevere.
insights.speaker: Alexander Gabuev
insights.so_what: The gap between the private admission of problems and the public dismissal is the tell — Moscow's stated pain threshold is not its actual one, so escalating strike campaigns retain leverage.
insights.quote: These terrorist attacks have no impact whatsoever on the situation
insights.locator: But Russians would adapt and persevere

insights.claim: The authors signal that Putin's confidence would have read differently 20 months earlier, implying Russia's underlying position has materially weakened even as its negotiating posture has hardened.
insights.speaker: Alexander Gabuev
insights.so_what: Weakness plus intransigence is the worst combination for settlement odds — attrition, not bargaining, remains the operative mechanism.
